title: Queues, topics and brokers
summary: Point-to-point versus publish-subscribe, consumer groups, delivery guarantees, and where Kafka and RabbitMQ fit.

steps.title: Queues and topics
body: Messaging systems offer two kinds of channel:
- **Queue (point-to-point)**: each message is delivered to **one** consumer. Several consumers on the same
queue **compete** for messages, which spreads the load. Use it for **commands**: "pick order A1".
- **Topic (publish-subscribe)**: each message is delivered to **every subscription**. Use it for **events**:
"order A1 shipped" interests billing, email and analytics.
Inside one subscription you can again have competing consumers. That is the model behind **Kafka consumer
groups** and behind **RabbitMQ** exchanges bound to one queue per subscriber.
Synchronous request-reply can also run over messaging: the request carries a `replyTo` address and a
**correlation id**, and the reply is matched back by that id.

items: Send `PickOrder A1` to the warehouse workers
Announce `OrderShipped` to billing, email and analytics
Resize uploaded cover images with five workers
Hand one invoice to the billing system to post

steps.title: Kafka and RabbitMQ at a glance
body: | | **RabbitMQ** | **Apache Kafka** |

| Model | broker routes messages from **exchanges** to **queues**; consumers acknowledge and the message is removed | an append-only **log** split into **partitions**; consumers track their own **offset** |
| Replay | gone once acknowledged | kept for a retention period; a new consumer can read from the start |
| Ordering | per queue | per **partition** (so pick the key that must stay ordered, e.g. the order id) |
| Scaling consumers | more consumers on a queue | up to one consumer per partition per group |
| Typical use | task queues, commands, request-reply | event streams, many readers, high volume, replay |
Camel speaks both (`rabbitmq:` / `spring-rabbitmq:` and `kafka:` components), as do JMS brokers and cloud services
such as Azure Service Bus.

steps.prompt: A Kafka topic has **2 partitions**. A consumer group runs **3 consumers**. What happens?
options: Two consumers each own one partition; the third is idle until a rebalance gives it work
Each consumer gets a third of the messages
steps.explain: Within a group a partition has one owner at a time. The partition count caps a group's parallelism, so size it for the consumers you expect.

steps.title: Delivery guarantees
body: - **At-most-once**: acknowledge before processing. A crash loses the message. Fine for metrics you can afford to drop.
- **At-least-once**: acknowledge after processing. A crash causes a **redelivery**, so duplicates happen.
This is the default you should design for.
- **Exactly-once**: only inside one system's transaction boundary (Kafka transactions, a database).
Across systems, the practical answer is **at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer**, sometimes called
*effectively once*.

steps.prompt: Match the guarantee to its failure mode.
pairs: A crash can lose a message
A crash can deliver a message twice
Duplicates arrive but are detected and skipped

steps.prompt: Three workers compete on one queue. What does this print?
steps.explain: Competing consumers share the work: each message goes to exactly one of them.

steps.title: A tiny broker
prompt: Model topics with consumer groups (the Kafka shape; a RabbitMQ queue per subscriber behaves the same).
- `void Subscribe(string topic, string group, string consumer)`: adds a consumer to a group on a topic. Groups and topics are created on first use. Keep consumers in the order they subscribed.

- `List<string> Publish(string topic, string message)`: delivers the message **once to every group** on the topic, to **one consumer** in each group, chosen round-robin per group (first message to the group's first consumer, next to the second, and so on, wrapping around). Return the deliveries as `"{group}/{consumer}: {message}"`, groups in the order they first subscribed. A topic with no groups returns an empty list.
starter: public void Subscribe(string topic, string group, string consumer) { }
public List<string> Publish(string topic, string message)
solution: public void Subscribe(string topic, string group, string consumer)
if (!topics.TryGetValue(topic, out var groups)) topics[topic] = groups = new();
if (g is null) groups.Add(g = new Group { Name = group });
public List<string> Publish(string topic, string message)
if (!topics.TryGetValue(topic, out var groups)) return result;
hints: Per topic, keep a list of groups; per group, a list of consumers and a counter.
template: Dojo.Eq("every group gets the event once", new List<string> { "billing/b1: A1", "email/e1: A1" }, dojoB.Publish("order-shipped", "A1"));
Dojo.Eq("round-robin inside a group", new List<string> { "billing/b1: A2", "email/e2: A2" }, dojoB.Publish("order-shipped", "A2"));
Dojo.Eq("round-robin wraps around", new List<string> { "billing/b1: A3", "email/e1: A3" }, dojoB.Publish("order-shipped", "A3"));
Dojo.Eq("topics are independent", new List<string> { "warehouse/w1: P1" }, dojoB.Publish("pick-order", "P1"));
Dojo.Eq("unknown topic delivers nothing", new List<string>(), dojoB.Publish("nobody", "x"));
